components.gap: Preserve the identified source variant of the definition (success condition not met: the source's form is replaced by a narrower one). Durrett (PTE5 sec. 4.6, p. 244) defines uniform integrability for an arbitrary collection of random variables X_i, i in I, with no integrability hypothesis, and remarks that choosing M with the supremum below one gives sup_i E|X_i| <= M+1 < infinity, a bound he says is used several times below; integrability of every member is thus a consequence of the defining limit, not an assumption. def:p15-uniform-integrability (body 15-22) instead restricts the definition to families of real integrable variables, adding the hypothesis that the source's remark makes unnecessary, and the reader text never states the arbitrary-collection form or that the defining limit itself forces sup_i E|X_i| < infinity (so that a collection with a member of infinite mean is not uniformly integrable). The bound appears only inside the annex proof of thm:p15-ui-small-sets (annex 5-7), for families already assumed integrable.

Preserve the identified source variant of Theorem 4.6.2 and its framing (success condition not met: narrowed hypothesis; failure condition: unstated assumption or unwritten step). Durrett (p. 245) introduces the criterion as a common way to check uniform integrability and states it for any function phi >= 0 with phi(x)/x -> infinity, assuming only E phi(|X_i|) <= C for all i, with no integrability hypothesis on the X_i (their integrability follows from the bound). thm:p15-ui-moment-criteria (body 48-55) narrows the hypothesis to finite Borel Phi. Because def:p15-uniform-integrability applies only to families of integrable variables, the theorem either presupposes integrability of the X_i (a hypothesis the source does not make) or owes its derivation, and the annex proof (annex 36-46) bounds E(|X_i|; |X_i| > M_eps) <= eps C without writing that E|X_i| < infinity follows. The source's statement that this criterion is a common way to check uniform integrability is not supplied. The two examples and the convex converse (body 52-59, annex 44-72) are written in full.

State and use only supplied hypotheses (failure condition: unstated assumption). thm:p15-submartingale-ui (body 110-121) is stated for any submartingale in the sense of def:p15-filtration-martingale (martingales-and-convergence.tex 18-25), which defines adaptedness but does not require it, and this chapter states no adaptedness convention (unlike martingale-maximal-inequalities.tex 16-17 and optional-stopping-and-random-walks.tex 12-13). The proof nevertheless uses adaptedness: annex 204-206 makes the convergence event and the chosen limit F_infinity-measurable because the limsup and liminf of the measurable variables are measurable, which needs every X_n to be F_infinity-measurable; annex 217-221 integrates over the F_n-events where E(X_infinity|F_n) - X_n <= -1/k, which needs X_n to be F_n-measurable; and annex 213 takes m = n in E(X_m|F_n) >= X_n. The F_infinity-measurable choice of X_infinity and the terminal inequality X_n <= E(X_infinity|F_n), with its supermartingale reversal (body 114-120), are therefore proved only under an assumption the theorem and the route's definition do not state. The equivalences of source Theorem 4.6.4 (p. 246) are otherwise written.

State and use only supplied hypotheses (failure condition: unstated assumption). annex 234-235 concludes that X_n is a version of E(X_infinity|F_n) since X_n is integrable and F_n-measurable, but under def:p15-filtration-martingale (martingales-and-convergence.tex 18-25) a martingale term is only almost surely equal to the F_n-measurable E(X_{n+1}|F_n), and this chapter assumes no completeness of sub-sigma-algebras (body 32-33), so F_n-measurability of X_n is an unstated assumption. The equivalence of the first three conditions (annex 228) and the F_infinity-measurable limit version used to identify X_infinity = E(Z|F_infinity) (annex 239-240) rest on the adaptedness-dependent steps of thm:p15-submartingale-ui (annex 204-206, 217-221). Lemmas 4.6.5-4.6.6 and Theorem 4.6.7 of the source (pp. 246-247) are otherwise written in full.

Supply the full treatment the entry cites as thm. 4.6.9 and continuation (omitted justificatory, historical and normative claims of the cited extent). After Theorem 4.6.9 Durrett (pp. 247-248) quotes Chung's invitation to judge whether the result is obvious or incredible, argues the obvious reading (1_A is F_infinity-measurable and F_n increases to F_infinity, so the best guess of 1_A given F_n should approach the best guess given F_infinity, which is 1_A), presents the Kolmogorov zero-one argument as the incredible reading, and closes with the evaluation that this argument may not show the theorem to be too unusual or improbable to be possible but that it and the later applications show it to be a very useful result. thm:p15-levy-information-law (body 161-176, annex 287-305) supplies the theorem, its L^1 form and the Kolmogorov proof only; the two-reading discussion with its attribution to Chung, the obvious reading as an interpretive claim, and the usefulness evaluation are not supplied.

Supply the full treatment promised by the declared status 'These are the complete source Exercises 4.6.2-3' (body 253) (omitted normative claim of the cited exercise). Durrett's Exercise 4.6.3 (p. 249) ends with the claim that this approximation is much simpler than the bare-hands approach of his Exercise 1.4.3 but uses a lot of machinery; the entry (body 229-254, annex 392-456) proves the approximation but does not state this comparison of the martingale route with the direct route. The mathematics of Exercises 4.6.2-4.6.3, the endpoint b = 1 and the completed-Lebesgue extension are written.

Supply the entry's definitions and the source's statistical reading of Exercise 4.6.1 (success condition not met: the entry's terms are undefined; omitted interpretive claim). Durrett (p. 248) states that with normal(0,1) noise the observations Y_1, Y_2, ... are, in statistical terms, a sample from a normal population with variance 1 and unknown mean, that the distribution of theta is called the prior distribution, and that P(theta in . | Y_1, ..., Y_n) is called the posterior distribution after n observations. thm:p15-posterior-mean-consistency (body 256-270) speaks of an integrable prior variable and of an unrestricted posterior consistency claim without defining the prior or the posterior distribution or referring to a definition of them on the route, and gives the normal case only as independent normal (0,1) noise, not as a sample from a normal population with variance 1 and unknown mean. The convergence claim and its proof (annex 458-479) are written.

Supply the source's terminology and justificatory claim at the opening of Section 4.7 (p. 249) (omitted historical and justificatory claims of the cited extent). Durrett notes that some authors call backwards martingales reversed, and justifies their separate treatment by the claim that, because the sigma-fields decrease as n decreases to minus infinity, the convergence theory for backwards martingales is particularly simple. def:p15-backward-martingale (body 315-330) supplies the definition and the translation to the source's negative indices, but the reader text states neither the alternative name (present only as the index entry martingale!reverse, body 329) nor the claim and its reason; thm:p15-backward-martingale-convergence (body 332-342) states the unconditional convergence without that reason.
